items.title: Active Recall: Close the Notes and Make Memory Work

Then check it, fix the misses, and practice application separately if the real goal is solving, speaking, writing, or doing. Familiarity feels nice; retrieval tells you what is actually available without the page in front of you. Choose a small set of material you want to retain. Hide the source and answer a question, explain the idea, or write what you remember. Check immediately enough to catch errors and repair them. Then, if success means solving, writing, speaking, calculating, or performing, practice that outcome too. Memory practice is useful; it is not a teleportation device to skill. items.title: Ask a Few Questions Before You Start Learning
items.search_text: Ask a Few Questions Before You Start Learning Before reading, watching, or studying new material, try a few questions about the specific information you want to learn. Attempt an answer, then study and check it. Evidence supports better learning for the prequestioned information, not a general boost to everything else. Choose a small set of questions that point to information you genuinely want to learn. Before opening the explanation, reading the chapter, or watching the lesson, make a brief attempt at each answer even if you are unsure. Then study normally, paying attention when the material resolves those questions. Afterward, check the answers against the source. Use this to target important information, not as a claim that every unasked detail will also be learned better. After studying, can I answer the questions accurately without looking, and did the questions point me toward information that actually mattered? learning-thinking Learning & Thinking memory Memory skill-learning Skill Learning metacognition Metacognition

items.title: Ask AI for Failure Cases Before You Ship
items.search_text: Ask AI for Failure Cases Before You Ship Give AI a feature, process, calculation, message, or workflow and ask for edge cases and failure modes. Treat the output as a candidate list, deduplicate it, verify relevance, and convert the useful cases into executable tests or checklist items. Describe the intended behavior, constraints, known happy path, and expensive failures. Ask for boundary cases, invalid inputs, state transitions, concurrency or timing issues where relevant, and user misunderstandings. Remove duplicates, verify each candidate against the real system, and write tests for the cases worth keeping. items.title: Batch Non-Urgent Notifications Instead of Receiving Them All Day
items.search_text: Batch Non-Urgent Notifications Instead of Receiving Them All Day Group non-urgent smartphone notifications into a few predictable delivery windows while keeping genuinely urgent channels available. The useful idea is predictable batching, not a magic number of batches. Choose the apps whose alerts are useful but rarely urgent. Use your phone's notification summary, scheduled focus mode, or another reversible setting to deliver those alerts in predictable windows. Keep calls, selected contacts, security alerts, calendars, or other genuinely time-sensitive channels outside the batch. items.title: Before You Commit to a Judgment, Consider the Opposite
items.search_text: Before You Commit to a Judgment, Consider the Opposite When a judgment matters and you already feel convinced, deliberately generate a plausible explanation, evidence pattern, or outcome that would point the other way. Use it as a bias check, not as a rule to distrust every conclusion. Write your current conclusion in one sentence. Then ask: what evidence, mechanism, or alternative explanation could make the opposite conclusion reasonable? Generate a concrete alternative rather than telling yourself to be objective. Check whether your decision would change if that alternative were true. Use this on decisions where biased assimilation or one-sided hypothesis testing is a real risk; do not turn it into endless doubt about routine choices. items.title: Judge a Commitment by What Comes Next

Name the decision. Separate unrecoverable past cost from future cost. List the realistic benefit of continuing, the best alternative use of the same resources, and any obligation or switching cost that genuinely exists now. items.search_text: Leave a Ready-to-Resume Note Before You Switch Tasks When you must leave unfinished work, capture where you stopped, the next concrete action, and one critical restart detail before switching. The goal is a cleaner return, not eliminating every cost of interruption. Use this only when unfinished work is about to be interrupted or deliberately parked. items.title: Make a Specific Repair Attempt After a Workable Conflict
items.search_text: Make a Specific Repair Attempt After a Workable Conflict After a misunderstanding or conflict where it is safe to re-engage, make a specific repair attempt: name what you did, acknowledge the likely impact without arguing about intent, apologize for your part, offer a concrete corrective action, and invite the other person's view. Acknowledge the impact as you understand it without using your intention to cancel the other person's experience. Apologize for your part without an 'if'. items.title: Move Caffeine Earlier When Sleep Matters
items.search_text: Move Caffeine Earlier When Sleep Matters If caffeine may be reaching into the night, move the last dose earlier and reduce large late-day doses. A 2025 randomized crossover trial found that a single 400 mg dose disrupted several sleep measures even when taken many hours before bed; a small 100 mg dose did not show a significant effect at the tested timings. That is a reason to be dose-aware, not a license for one universal cutoff. For one or two weeks, note the time and rough amount of your last caffeine, your bedtime, and whether sleep onset, overnight restfulness, and next-day sleepiness are broadly better or worse. Start by moving the last large dose earlier or reducing it; do not deliberately take caffeine late just to test your tolerance. items.search_text: Pair a Useful Task with Something You Genuinely Want Pair a beneficial activity that is easy to postpone with a compatible pleasure you already enjoy. Choose one 'should' behavior that is useful but easy to delay and one 'want' experience that can happen at the same time without making the task worse. Examples might include a favorite audiobook during a walk or routine cardio, a preferred podcast while doing repetitive household work, or another compatible pairing. items.title: Pause Long Enough to Notice a Good Moment
items.search_text: Pause Long Enough to Notice a Good Moment When something genuinely pleasant is already happening, give it a little deliberate attention instead of rushing past it. This is a conservative savoring practice, not a rule to feel positive or reinterpret difficult experiences. Choose a positive experience that is already real: a good meal, a joke, a quiet walk, finishing useful work, music, a kind message, or another ordinary moment. For a short period, stop adding new input. Notice one or two concrete details and what makes the moment worth noticing. Then continue your day. items.title: Protect Enough Sleep Opportunity and Track Daytime Function
items.search_text: Protect Enough Sleep Opportunity and Track Daytime Function If your sleep is routinely short, protect a realistic window that gives you enough opportunity to sleep and observe simple trends in sleep timing and daytime alertness. Do not deliberately restrict sleep to search for an 'optimal' number or treat one bad night as a result. Choose a bedtime-to-wake window that fits your obligations and gives you a reasonable opportunity for enough sleep. For a week or two, record only a few things: roughly when you tried to sleep, when you got up, whether the night was unusually disrupted, and how alert or sleepy you felt during the day. Look for repeated patterns, not single-night scores. Change one practical constraint at a time, such as moving bedtime earlier when your current schedule routinely leaves too little time for sleep. items.search_text: Structure Dense Writing for Fast Navigation Turn a dense draft into a navigable document by giving each section one job and choosing headings, tables, diagrams, or images according to the information the reader needs to inspect. items.title: Take a Short Walk When Stress Builds
items.search_text: Take a Short Walk When Stress Builds Whenever stress hits, take a quick 10-minute walk—whether it’s outside, around a park, or just circling your office. When stress is building, consider a short, comfortable walk if walking is safe and practical for you. Treat ten minutes as a convenient boundary, not a medically proven dose. If a greener route is just as easy and safe, prefer it as a reasonable experiment rather than making a special trip. Then notice whether you feel any different before returning to the next task. Pick an ordinary low-pressure interaction that already needs to happen: buying coffee, greeting a neighbor, talking to a receptionist, or another brief exchange. items.title: Use a High-Intensity Interval Timer Safely

items.title: Use AI to Scaffold Code, Then Make Tests Decide
items.search_text: Use AI to Scaffold Code, Then Make Tests Decide Use AI to produce a first implementation for a bounded coding task, then inspect the diff, run tests, add missing edge cases, and reject code you cannot explain. A controlled experiment found faster completion on one coding task; it did not establish universal software quality gains. Define the behavior and constraints first. Ask AI for a small implementation. Read the diff, run the existing test suite, add tests for edge cases and failure paths, and inspect security or data-handling implications. Keep only code you can explain and maintain. Did AI shorten implementation time without increasing code I do not understand, test, or want to own? work-money Work & Money work-systems Work Systems

items.title: Use AI to Widen the Idea Set Before You Choose
items.search_text: Use AI to Widen the Idea Set Before You Choose When you are stuck on the first obvious idea, use AI to generate alternatives across different assumptions or constraints. Experimental evidence suggests generative AI can raise judged creativity in some ideation tasks; it does not decide which idea fits your real context. State the problem and constraints. Ask for several directions that must differ from one another in a named way. Cluster similar answers, discard obvious filler, and evaluate the remaining options against real constraints and evidence. Did AI add genuinely different options, or merely rephrase the same idea several times? creativity-expression Creativity & Expression idea-generation Idea Generation creative-problem-solving Creative Problem Solving

items.title: Use AI to Widen the Option Set, Not Make the Decision
items.search_text: Use AI to Widen the Option Set, Not Make the Decision When a decision feels binary or prematurely settled, ask AI for plausible alternatives, missing criteria, and arguments against your current favorite. Verify factual claims independently and keep the final weighting of trade-offs human. Write your objective, constraints, and current leading option. Ask AI for materially different alternatives, missing criteria, and the strongest case against your favorite. items.title: Use AIDA as a Message Clarity Checklist
items.search_text: Use AIDA as a Message Clarity Checklist Check whether a message earns attention, makes the relevant point understandable, explains why it matters, and gives the reader a clear next action without treating AIDA as a persuasion guarantee. Name the audience and desired next step, review the opening for relevance, remove information that does not help understanding, explain the concrete value or consequence honestly, and end with one clear action the reader can accept, decline, or ignore. items.title: Use an Extreme Seed, Then Return to Reality
items.search_text: Use an Extreme Seed, Then Return to Reality Start an idea session with a deliberately unrealistic seed, explore its consequences without defending it and then translate useful fragments back into real constraints. State the real problem. Choose an extreme seed that changes one constraint, customer, resource or rule. During a short generation round, list consequences and variants without arguing with the seed. items.title: Use the 20-20-20 Rule for Screen Breaks
items.search_text: Use the 20-20-20 Rule for Screen Breaks When you spend a long time looking at screens, take a short distance-viewing break: about every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet away for 20 seconds. During long periods of screen use, take a short visual break about every 20 minutes and look at something about 20 feet away for 20 seconds. items.search_text: Use WOOP to Turn a Wish Into an If-Then Plan Use a Wish, desired Outcome, likely internal Obstacle, and a concrete if-then Plan to make one meaningful goal easier to act on. Treat the method as a self-regulation tool, not a guarantee of goal achievement. Choose one meaningful and reasonably feasible wish. Describe the outcome you want, identify an internal obstacle that could derail you, then write: If I notice this obstacle, then I will take this specific action. items.title: Use Your Senses to Return to the Present
items.search_text: Use Your Senses to Return to the Present Spend 3–5 minutes focusing on your senses. Notice what you see, hear, smell, feel, and taste. items.title: Walk Soon After a Meal When You Would Otherwise Sit
items.search_text: Walk Soon After a Meal When You Would Otherwise Sit When it is safe and practical, replace some sitting after a meal with comfortable walking.
